tweets.text:
The people actually building the AI infrastructure are describing incredible demand and a multi-year supply shortage. The market is worrying about a bubble.  

$AMZN CEO Andy Jassy: Even with $220B in 2026 capex, Amazon is still leaving meaningful demand on the table. 2026 sold out. 2027 largely sold out. Good chunk of 2028 already booked.  

$SPCX CEO Elon Musk: Demand is overwhelming supply. New compute is paying back in under a year. Shortage will last a long time. Power and construction are the real bottlenecks.  

$NVDA CEO Jensen Huang: Neocloud demand is “off the charts.” Orders keep coming. Bottlenecks keep shifting (chips → packaging → HBM → power) and will last for years. The missing piece is capital, not demand.  

Stocks are down because of financing stress, higher rates and FCF optics - not because utilisation, backlog or rental pricing collapsed.   

When operators with the best visibility are still constrained and sold out well into 2027–28, the recent selloff looks more like a positioning reset than a demand air-pocket.  

This is usually when the better opportunities show up. Remember the adage "Buy fear, sell euphoria."

tweets.text:
The current generation of models is already really good at coding. The next generation will be even better. As often happens, the capabilities are there before someone builds the harness to fully use them.

I think we’re going to get an OpenClaw moment for software replication. Someone will drop a simple harness that:

- Visits a software product with computer use, clicks everywhere, fills out forms and explores every workflow.
-Inspects the DOM, console logs, network requests, API responses and how state changes to figure out how it works.
-Turns those observations into tests covering the UI and the backend behavior it can observe.
-Writes a giant Markdown TODO and launches a swarm of agents to rebuild it.
-Uses the browser again to run the same workflows against both versions, compare results and keep fixing the differences.

Give it a URL, let it run. Software competition is going to get very close to perfect competition.

tweets.text:
Never doubt the AI exponential, because it can catch up with your entire career while you’re still explaining why your profession is special.

Just listened to Cédric Villani, a Fields Medal winner, talking about how shocked he was by the progress of AI. Funny because I met him twice, including around 2018 when he was a Member of Parliament leading France’s AI mission, and we were already discussing how fast NLP was progressing with the new transformers.

France has 13 Fields Medals, second only to the US, and some of the brightest people I know come from that world. A lot of them have been caught by surprise despite following AI for years and using the products themselves.

I think it’s very hard to accept the exponential when it threatens something you’ve spent your entire life building, especially when your career is such a big part of your identity. You can see what’s happening to graphic designers or software engineers and still convince yourself that your own work will take another 20 years.

My guess is every intellectual profession will go through this, and honestly, even believing in the exponential doesn’t prepare you for the consequences. I work on this stuff all day, I expect progress to keep compounding, and I still struggle to imagine what that means a few years from now.

I don’t think nature has equipped us to really grasp exponential growth. We can understand the math and still struggle to imagine what it means for our own lives, even while watching it happen.

The last 10 years of SaaS were about standardizing software. Build one great experience, sell it to millions of users, enjoy high gross margins.

The next 10 years will be about personalizing it. Everyone gets software that works exactly the way they want.

“I hate my screenshot tool.” Build a new one. “I want my mailbox organized differently.” Rebuild it.

People loved OpenClaw because it felt magical to have an assistant that remembers them and gets things done. Imagine when that assistant can also build whatever software they need.

The next few months are going to be wild.
